title: LaPorte, Indiana: the LaPorte Weather Anomaly
notes: From the queue (Scoop, Nov. 13: weather history). A real weather mystery, not a ghost story. The 31% / 38% / 246% figures are for 1951-1965 only (not 'since 1925'). The cause is what Changnon 'suggested'; the critics 'questioned the observer's records' (Holzman and Thom's own text wasn't read, so no 'fraud'). METROMEX left out (only Changnon's group says La Porte inspired it). No press quotes (none found with two sources). Blind check Nov. 21: line 1 was overstated ('steel mills were making it storm'), now 'industry near Chicago was adding to the rain and storms'; 30 miles is to the Gary-South Chicago industry (Huff and Changnon: 25-35 mi), so the map has no Chicago pin; 'faded' with no decade (1960s per Changnon 1980; after 1970 per Niyogi and Schmid 2014); 'never fully settled'; no weather-office picture (the records were one cooperative observer's) and no oil lamp. Second check: 'heat' dropped (not confirmed as Changnon's), 'ROUGHLY 30 MILES'.

sources.what: title 'The La Porte Weather Anomaly—Fact or Fiction?', Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society 49(1), 1968; 'A notable increase in precipitation, moderate rain days, thunderstorm days, and hail days has been occurring since 1925'; 'during the 1951–1965 period La Porte had 31% more precipitation, 38% more thunderstorms ... and 246% more hail days than did surrounding stations'; about 30 miles east of heavy industry, suggesting 'inadvertent' modification; precipitation follows Chicago steel production
sources.who: S. A. Changnon Jr., BAMS, 1968 (abstract, AMS and Scilit)

sources.what: 'For the period of 1951-1965, Changnon reported positive anomalies at La Porte of 31% for mean precipitation and 38% for the number of thunderstorm days'; 'about 30 miles downwind of the industrial complex of Gary'; 'transport of rainfall-augmenting pollutants by prevailing winds'; Holzman and Thom (1970): 'observer-perpetuated and fictional'; Changnon: 'not substantiated'; 'remains debatable'

beats.text: A scientist once suggested that industry near Chicago was adding to the rain and storms over LaPorte, Indiana.
beats.label: LAPORTE, INDIANA
beats.credit: History: Changnon, Bulletin of the American Meteorological Society, 1968

beats.text: He published his findings in 1968, in a leading weather journal.

card.paper: BULLETIN OF THE AMERICAN METEOROLOGICAL SOCIETY

beats.credit: Changnon, BAMS 49(1), 1968; Norwine, Indiana Academy of Science

beats.text: From 1951 to 1965, he reported, LaPorte got 31% more precipitation and 38% more thunderstorms than stations around it.
beats.label: 1951 TO 1965
beats.credit: Changnon, BAMS, 1968; Norwine, Indiana Academy of Science

beats.label: HAIL DAYS
beats.credit: Changnon, BAMS, 1968; Huff and Changnon, Illinois State Water Survey, 1972

beats.text: LaPorte sits about 30 miles downwind of the industry around Chicago and Gary. He suggested its pollution was feeding the storms.
beats.label: ROUGHLY 30 MILES DOWNWIND
beats.credit: Changnon, BAMS, 1968; Norwine, Indiana Academy of Science; Cassity, MIT, 1969

beats.text: Other scientists pushed back. They questioned the local weather observer's records.
beats.label: THE CRITICS, 1970
beats.credit: Norwine, Indiana Academy of Science; Changnon, Journal of Weather Modification

beats.text: Later, the anomaly faded. It was never fully settled how much of it was real.
beats.label: NEVER SETTLED
beats.credit: Changnon, BAMS, 1980; Cassity, MIT, 1969; Ashby and Fritts, BAMS, 1972

beats.text: Comment your town, and it could be next.
